domain: ML model evaluation methodology and capability-benchmark provenance for automated routing/selection systems
axioms: A benchmark score is only a valid routing input if it is comparable across the vendors being compared — same harness, same task version, same scoring method; a raw number without that metadata is not a fact, it is an artifact of one specific eval run.

Provenance tagging (benchmark | judgment | unknown) is only meaningful if the tag survives every transformation in the pipeline (snapshot -> seed file -> registry -> decision function); a tag that can be silently dropped or coerced is decorative, not load-bearing.

A capability axis populated from a single data point (one model, one study, one flag) is not yet a measured axis for the whole registry — it is an anecdote wearing a schema's clothing until coverage exists across candidates.

Multi-axis capability vectors have no natural total order; a routing system that consumes vectors must define an explicit dominance/tie-break rule, or the 'decision' for non-dominated cases is arbitrary and effectively untested.

Any system built to fix 'facts are stale' must itself be checked for staleness at authoring time — inheriting the problem while claiming to solve it is the single most common failure of a facts-refresh project.
Drift detection without a defined threshold, cadence, or owner is equivalent to no drift detection — a report nobody is obligated to read is not a control.
'Unknown treated conservatively' is a policy statement, not a mechanism; it only holds if 'conservative' is defined precisely enough that two implementers would build the same behavior from it.
primitives: benchmark result (score, harness version, task version, eval date)
capability vector (a model's position across all axes)
dominance / tie-break rule (how a vector-valued comparison resolves to one decision)
drift (divergence between registry value and current source-of-truth over time)
failure_mode: Reasons about whether a capability claim is well-sourced but tends not to check whether the resulting routing decision is even computable (dominance/tie-break logic) — that gap sits at the boundary with policy-engine design and can fall through if not explicitly pulled into scope.

Focuses on the correctness/comparability of individual facts and may under-weight structural questions like whether the schema key for a benchmark result includes enough metadata (harness/version) to detect future incomparability — that is a schema-design concern this lens borders but doesn't own.

Can over-index on the specific benchmarks named in a document (Terminal-Bench, SWE-Bench Pro) and under-index on the general pattern (single-vendor research flag treated as a universal axis) if the review isn't pushed to generalize beyond the cited examples.
